title: Proof by Contradiction
short: Assume the statement is false and reason to something impossible, as in the proof that √2 is irrational.
trouble: Students start from a wrong negation of the statement, so the contradiction they reach proves nothing.

blocks.html: Some statements, like "$\sqrt{2}$ is irrational" from the real number system, say that something does not exist. There is nothing to start a direct proof from. Proof by contradiction supplies a starting point: assume the opposite and watch it fall apart. It is a cousin of proof by contrapositive.

To prove $S$ by contradiction, assume $ eg S$ and reason until you reach something impossible, a statement and its negation together. Since $ eg S$ leads to a contradiction, $ eg S$ is false, so $S$ is true. The assumption must be the exact negation of $S$; to prove "if $P$, then $Q$," assume $P$ and $ eg Q$.

If $ eg S o (R \wedge eg R)$ is true, then $ eg S$ must be false, because $R \wedge eg R$ is false in every row, and a true conditional with a false conclusion must have a false hypothesis. This is why the negation must be exact: a contradiction reached from the wrong assumption only shows that the wrong assumption is false, which tells you nothing about $S$. The rules for negating quantifiers are the tool for getting it right.

blocks.title: $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational
steps: Suppose not: $\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}$ for integers $a$, $b$ with $b \ne 0$, and the fraction in lowest terms (any fraction can be reduced).
Square: $2 = \frac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}$, so $a^{2} = 2b^{2}$. Then $a^{2}$ is even, so $a$ is even (the contrapositive lesson proved this). Write $a = 2c$.
Substitute: $4c^{2} = 2b^{2}$, so $b^{2} = 2c^{2}$. Now $b^{2}$ is even, so $b$ is even.
Both $a$ and $b$ are even, so $\frac{a}{b}$ was not in lowest terms: a contradiction. So $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
blocks.a: The assumption forces $a$ and $b$ both even, contradicting lowest terms.

blocks.title: There are infinitely many primes
blocks.q: Prove that there are infinitely many primes.
steps: Suppose not: the primes are exactly $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{k}$.
Let $N = p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{k} + 1$. Dividing $N$ by any $p_{i}$ leaves remainder $1$, so no $p_{i}$ divides $N$.
But $N > 1$, so $N$ has some prime factor, and that prime is not on the list. This contradicts "the list has every prime."
Note that $N$ itself need not be prime: $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 + 1 = 30{,}031 = 59 \cdot 509$. The proof only needs a prime factor that is new.
blocks.a: Any finite list of primes misses a prime factor of $N$.

blocks.title: No largest even integer
blocks.q: Prove that there is no largest even integer.
steps: Then $N + 2$ is even (it is $2(k + 1)$ if $N = 2k$) and larger than $N$.
That contradicts "$N$ is the largest." So no largest even integer exists.
blocks.a: $N + 2$ beats any proposed largest even integer.

blocks.html: Starting from a wrong negation. To prove "if $n^{2}$ is even, then $n$ is even," the assumption must be "$n^{2}$ is even and $n$ is odd." Assuming "$n^{2}$ is odd" or "$n$ is even" negates the wrong thing, and any contradiction you reach proves nothing about the original claim. Check: write the claim in symbols, negate it with the rules ($ eg(P o Q) \equiv P \wedge eg Q$, $ eg orall \equiv \exists eg$), and start from exactly that.
